prompt: What does the rational decision model assume?

options.text: The decision maker can identify and evaluate all alternatives and all their consequences
The decision maker picks the first satisfactory solution
Decisions are negotiated between coalitions
Preferences emerge during the decision process

explanation: Rational choice (classical economics) assumes complete knowledge of alternatives and consequences → optimal decision. b is Simon's satisficing, c the Carnegie model.

prompt: Which elements limit rationality according to Herbert Simon?

options.text: Incomplete and imperfect information
Limited information-processing capacity
Limited time for decision-making
Preferences that are not clearly predefined
An excess of reliable information that cannot be ignored

explanation: Simon: information incomplete, limited processing capacity and selective perception, limited time, preferences not predefined. Too much information is not one of his limits.

options.text: choosing the first satisfactory and sufficient solution
choosing the solution that satisfies all stakeholders equally
choosing the optimal solution after comparing all alternatives
postponing the decision until all information is available

explanation: Simon replaces optimisation criteria with satisfactory performance criteria: the first good-enough solution wins.

prompt: Which statements describe bounded rationality rather than the rational model?

options.text: Sequential search for alternatives
Synoptic evaluation of all alternatives
The solution respects the organisational status quo
The “real world” model of how managers decide
Selection of the best course of action to optimise the firm's value system

explanation: Bounded rationality: sequential, satisficing, status quo, real world. Synoptic evaluation and optimisation belong to the rational model.

prompt: How do organisations help to overcome bounded rationality?

options.text: Division of labour reduces each person's attention and competency span
Hierarchy spares people from questioning the soundness of orders
Rules and procedures provide ready-made solutions
Information channels separate those who collect information from those who use it
They give every employee access to all information

explanation: Organisations are decision-support systems: division of labour, hierarchy and control, rules, information channels. They reduce complexity – not by giving everyone all information.

prompt: The Carnegie model of organisational decision-making is based on the work of …

options.text: Cyert, March & Simon
French & Raven
Crozier & Friedberg
Jones & George

explanation: Richard Cyert, James March and Herbert Simon, all at Carnegie-Mellon University.

prompt: Which statements fit the Carnegie model?

options.text: Large firms are coalitions of sub-groups with different interests
Goals are compromises negotiated by the sub-groups
The overall solution is the juxtaposition of local solutions
Top management defines one optimal goal that all sub-groups pursue
The process stops once a solution satisfactory to the hierarchy is found

explanation: Coalitions, negotiated goals in an implicit order of priority, sub-problems solved with standard procedures, satisficing, juxtaposition of local solutions. No single optimal goal.

prompt: Which are weaknesses of collective decision-making?

options.text: Social loafing and ambiguous responsibility
Group polarisation
Greater commitment to the decision
Sobriety of expression
More complete information and knowledge

explanation: Commitment and more complete information are strengths. Weaknesses: time, conformity, domination, social loafing, denial of intuition, sobriety of expression, polarisation, groupthink.

prompt: Which of the following are among Janis' eight symptoms of groupthink?

options.text: Illusion of invulnerability
Self-appointed mindguards
Illusion of unanimity
Social loafing
Belief in inherent morality

explanation: Social loafing is a general weakness of groups (Ringelmann), not one of Janis' eight groupthink symptoms.

prompt: A group is especially vulnerable to groupthink when …

options.text: its members have similar backgrounds
it is insulated from outside opinions
there are no clear rules for decision-making
it includes a designated devil's advocate and outside experts

explanation: Janis: similar backgrounds, insulation and missing decision rules. Outside experts and a devil's advocate counteract groupthink.

prompt: In Allison's political model, a decision is …

options.text: the output of negotiation and interplay between actors with specific interests
shaped by organisational processes, structure and culture
made by individuals with limited time and cognitive skills
the optimal choice of a unified rational actor

explanation: Political model: power games. b is the organisational model, c the bounded rationality model.

prompt: Which focus belongs to which of Allison's models? Select the correct pairs.

options.text: Bounded rationality model – biases
Organisational model – structure, culture, incentives
Political model – power games
Organisational model – power games

explanation: Bounded rationality → biases; organisational model → structure, culture, incentives; political model → power games.

statement: According to Simon, managers in the real world choose the optimal solution after evaluating all alternatives.
explanation: They choose the FIRST satisfactory and sufficient solution (satisficing), not the optimal one.

statement: The rational model of decision-making stems from classical economic theory.
explanation: It comes from economics (Adam Smith, Ricardo, Walras): decision as the result of intended rational choice.

statement: Herbert Simon received the Nobel Prize in economics for his bounded rationality model.
explanation: Simon (1916–2001) received the Nobel Prize in 1978.

statement: Under bounded rationality, decision-making is synoptic rather than sequential.
explanation: It is the other way round: sequential (one option after another), not synoptic (all at once).

statement: In the Carnegie model, the overall solution of the organisation is the simple juxtaposition of local solutions.
explanation: Each sub-group solves its sub-problem with its standard procedures and stops at a satisfactory solution; the local solutions are put side by side.

statement: Group polarisation means that groups tend to settle on moderate compromise decisions.
explanation: Polarisation radicalises decisions: with a shared normative orientation, persuasive arguments escalate and groups can adopt extreme attitudes.

statement: The term groupthink was coined by Irving Janis.
explanation: Janis (1972): faulty decisions resulting from pressure within the group.

statement: “Sobriety of expression” refers to group members minimising warning signals so as not to be the messenger of bad news.
explanation: Example from class: pilots and the control tower.

statement: In Allison's organisational model, the decision is mainly explained by power games between actors.
explanation: Power games are the political model. The organisational model focuses on structure, culture and incentives.

prompt: Compare the rational decision model with Simon's bounded rationality model. Why do organisations matter for decision-making?
modelAnswer:
Rational model (classical economics; Jones & George): the decision maker identifies and evaluates all alternatives and all their consequences, compares them synoptically and chooses the optimal course of action. Step by step: problem, objectives, data, all alternatives, best choice, implementation, feedback. It is an ideal – a utopia – because it ignores time constraints and the limits of human knowledge and information processing.
Bounded rationality (Simon, Nobel 1978): information is incomplete and imperfect, cognitive capacity and time are limited, preferences are not predefined, and not all alternatives and consequences can be known. Decision makers therefore satisfice: they search sequentially and choose the first satisfactory and sufficient solution, which respects the status quo and can be taken quickly. It is the “real world” model.
Organisations are decision-support systems that bring decisions closer to rationality: division of labour reduces each person's span of attention, hierarchy and control spare people from questioning orders, rules and procedures offer ready-made solutions, and information channels separate collection from use. They reduce complexity and absorb uncertainty.
keyPoints: Rational: all alternatives and consequences, optimal, synoptic – utopia
Simon: limits of information, cognition, time, preferences
Satisficing and sequential search, first satisfactory solution
Organisations as decision-support systems: division of labour, hierarchy, rules, information channels

prompt: What is groupthink? Present its symptoms and the conditions that make a group vulnerable to it, and suggest how a board could prevent it.
modelAnswer:
Groupthink (Irving Janis, 1972): a group makes faulty decisions because of “a deterioration of mental efficiency, reality testing and moral judgment resulting from pressure within the group”.
Eight symptoms: illusion of invulnerability (excessive optimism, extreme risks); collective rationalisation (warnings discounted); belief in inherent morality (ethical consequences ignored); stereotyped views of out-groups; direct pressure on dissenters; self-censorship; illusion of unanimity; self-appointed mindguards who shield the group and the leader from contradictory information.
Vulnerability: members with similar backgrounds, insulation from outside opinions, no clear rules for decision-making. Consequences: alternatives ignored, irrational actions, other groups dehumanised – e.g. Pearl Harbor, Bay of Pigs, Vietnam, Iraq.
Prevention (derived from the risk factors): diverse members, outside experts and opinions, clear decision rules, a devil's advocate, leader states his view last, anonymous voting.
keyPoints: Several of the 8 symptoms named and explained
Risk factors: similar backgrounds, insulation, no rules
Prevention linked to the risk factors

prompt: Apply Allison's three approaches to analyse the US decision in the Cuban Missile Crisis.
modelAnswer:
Allison (Essence of Decision, 1971) explains one decision through three lenses.
1 · Bounded rationality model (focus: biases): Kennedy and the ExComm decided under extreme time pressure with incomplete intelligence on the missiles and Soviet intentions. They could not evaluate all options and consequences and chose a satisfactory option – the naval blockade (“quarantine”) – rather than an optimised one; the choice was sequential and kept options open.
2 · Organisational model (focus: structure, culture, incentives): the options available were limited by what the Navy, Air Force and CIA could do with their existing routines and procedures (air-strike plans, blockade procedures). Each organisation proposed what its standard procedures allowed; the decision reflects these processes more than a free choice.
3 · Political model (focus: power games): the outcome was the result of bargaining between actors with different interests – military chiefs (hawks) pushing for air strikes or invasion vs advisers favouring diplomacy (doves) – and of negotiation between Kennedy and Khrushchev (withdrawal of missiles from Cuba against a no-invasion pledge and the later removal of US missiles from Turkey).
The three lenses complement each other; contrast with the Bay of Pigs (1961), a classic groupthink fiasco.
keyPoints: Bounded rationality: time pressure, incomplete information, satisfactory option (blockade)
Organisational model: options limited by routines of Navy, Air Force, CIA
Political model: hawks vs doves, Kennedy–Khrushchev bargaining
